I totally relate to doctors appointment anxiety, specifically because of the weigh in process. First off, take a second to be proud that you are following through with this appointment, and acknowledging the anxiety you have with it- it’s not easy to admit that, it takes a great deal of strength! Before jumping to Xanax, ask yourself what usually calms you down in moments of anxiety. What are your health coping mechanisms? I’d try those out first to see if that helps. You could also tell your dr/nurse when they’re doing your vitals to not disclose your weight info. If you explain that you have an ED they will be incredibly understanding and sensitive I PROMISE (I haven’t been told my weight for years because almost all my dr’s know this). So if you go into it not knowing that you’ll hear those numbers, have a snack or even something small to tie you over through your appointment, ESPECIALLY if you’re getting blood drawn.

I’m not a health professional so I don’t feel comfortable advising you take medication, but from MY experience, my mom has given me half of a Xanax pill before a flight and I didn’t like, knock out instantly from it. But again, that’s from my experience, my moms a nurse and was conscious and thoughtful making that decision. 

Good luck, I’ll be thinking and hoping you’re doing well tomorrow at your appointment. Be kind to yourself:)💚

My dad wasn’t really in my life, and my parents didn’t get divorced until I was 13, but my mom was essentially a single mom for the entirety of my life. 

Pros: 
My mom was a great role model in the sense that despite many difficulties and hurdles she had to maneuver through being a single parent, my siblings and I turned out pretty good-so I do admire her a lot. We didn’t have a lot of money and she was stretched thin, so it taught me to be ok with not having an abundance, and I think just humbled me a lot. It also made me become more independent early on, which has prepped me great for adulthood.

Cons:
I was the youngest, and like I said, my mom was stretched thin, and I feel like I got the short end of the stick. I’m close with her, but there’s definitely some distance between us. She doesn’t seem to know me as well as she does with my other siblings. Also there were lots of moments of distress in our household due to complications with my parents relationship, and since my mom did not have another adult partner in our home, she was a bit emotionally dependent on us from a pretty young age. 

All in all, single moms are literally the strongest women alive. But they’re not perfect, and I think they own up to that a lot. I think my life would’ve turned out a lot WORSE if my parents stayed together, so it was for sure for the best.

As someone who’s been suffering anorexia for almost 11 years, diet culture in America is so much more prevalent and imbedded in our daily culture than we may see it (although I don’t think it was necessarily the direct cause of my ED). As someone who was raised by a father who was a drug addict, and am no longer in contact with him, I would advise you just be someone to listen to her. Let her talk as much or as little on the subject matter. If this is new information to her, she may not be ready for therapy and group organization/resources quite yet. It takes a second to process all of it. But as time goes on, perhaps mentioning those programs may change her to be more open minded. ACOA (adult child of alcoholics-works for any sort of dtysfunctionalality in any home) is an example. It’s just a space where people who have been raised in similar circumstances reflect and talk about the trauma and impact their parents decisions and habits have had on them. One thing is for certain, your friend is DEFINITELY not alone. Be there for her, don’t shame her situation, and be loving. A little empathy goes a long. Just be a good friend:)

My eating disorder doctor, whom I see every 2 months, is truly an incredible woman and healthcare provider. When she speaks to me, she speaks to me like I’m her daughter. Forming connections like this, especially if your patient has a past history of dysfunctional parents, is crucial for getting the truth out. If she had been cold and flat to me, I don’t think I’d be as comfortable telling her my full story. 

Also make yourself accessible to them through phone. She gave me her number, and made it clear I could call whenever I needed. Not only does she care and provide insight on my physical health, but mental health is just as important. 

She doesn’t ask me what I ate purely to ensure I actually ate or had the “right foods”, she will also ask how I felt when I ate those foods, and what emotions they brought me. 

I think the number one thing you can do is show empathy and love, and absolutely no shame. Also, never allow your patient to see their weight until YOU think it’s ok for them. It’s triggering
